Empirical Research Plan:  Elderly AMI Patients, Intensive Early Treatment, and Survival

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Chosen design:  Two–Stage Least Squares (instrumental variables).

Rationale  
•  The main threat is non-random selection: patients who receive early invasive procedures tend to be younger, have fewer co-morbidities, present earlier, and/or are treated at better hospitals.  
•  A plausibly exogenous source of treatment variation is the “differential distance” to hospitals that aggressively employ early invasive procedures. In an emergency, AMI patients are typically taken to the nearest capable hospital; the extra miles to a high-intensity hospital are effectively random conditional on home ZIP code, ambulance service areas, and time of day.  
•  Distance instruments are continuous (strong first stage) and, conditional on geography fixed effects, satisfy the exclusion restriction because living slightly closer to a high-intensity hospital should not affect mortality except through the likelihood of receiving intensive treatment.

Secondary design (robustness):  event-study/DID around hospital adoption of catheterization labs.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
Treated = 1 if the patient receives any invasive cardiac procedure (catheterization, PCI, or CABG) within 24 hours of admission.  
A second, mutually exclusive variable distinguishes diagnostic-only catheterization from revascularization to study treatment components.

Control group  
Patients admitted with AMI who do **not** receive an invasive procedure within 24 hours (conservative management).  
Because the 2SLS design uses a continuous instrument, we do not have to pre-specify a separate “control hospital”; instead, every patient contributes, with treatment intensity instrumented by distance.

Treatment timing / event date  
Event = hospital admission for AMI (time 0).  Survival tracked at 30 days, 1 year, 5 years.

Instrument
Z = Differential distance =  (miles from the centroid of the patient’s home ZIP to the **nearest high-intensity hospital**)  –  
(miles to the **nearest low-intensity hospital**), where “high intensity” = top quartile of hospitals by fraction of AMI patients receiving early invasive therapy in the preceding calendar year.  
Smaller (negative) values ⇒ patient is relatively closer to a high-intensity provider ⇒ higher likelihood of treatment.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Instrument relevance (first-stage)  
Differential distance must strongly predict receipt of early invasive therapy.  Plausible because ambulance routing is highly sensitive to distance in emergencies.

A2. Exclusion restriction  
Conditional on geographic fixed effects and observable patient/hospital characteristics, differential distance affects mortality solely through its effect on early invasive therapy.  Plausible because travel distance of a few miles should not directly improve survival once the patient reaches a hospital.

A3. Independence / as-good-as-random assignment of instrument  
Living somewhat closer to a high-intensity hospital is unrelated to unobservable severity of the patient’s heart attack or general health after conditioning on ZIP-code socio-economic covariates and county*year fixed effects.

A4. Monotonicity  
No patient becomes **less** likely to receive intensive therapy by living closer to an intensive hospital (no “defiers”).  Reasonable in practice.

A5. SUTVA  
One patient’s instrument/treatment does not affect another’s survival (no spillovers).  Plausible given individual-level outcomes.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Spatial sorting of healthier seniors near high-tech hospitals.  
•  Mitigation: control for rich ZIP-code socio-economic and demographic variables; include county-by-year fixed effects; restrict sample to patients arriving by ambulance from the **same ZIP in which they reside**; robustness check using only rural areas where sorting is minimal.

T2. Selective hospital bypass by EMTs (e.g., sicker patients routed to tertiary centers irrespective of distance).  
•  Mitigation: condition on pre-hospital clinical severity (e.g., STEMI indicator, Killip class if available), time of day, weekend vs weekday; test balance of observable severity measures by instrument quantiles.

T3. Instrument affects outcomes through other hospital quality dimensions (high-intensity hospitals may also have better nursing ratios, ICU care, etc.).  
•  Mitigation: include hospital fixed effects interacted with calendar year where feasible (essentially comparing patients who, because of marginal distance differences, go to alternative hospitals with different propensities); test for effect of instrument on outcomes of **non-eligible diagnoses** (e.g., CHF admissions) as falsification.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# --- 0. Packages ---------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)     # fast data handling
library(fixest)         # high-performance IV regressions
library(modelsummary)   # nice tables
library(ggplot2)        # plots

# --- 1. Load data --------------------------------------------------
ami <- fread("ami_data.csv")   # each row = patient admission

# --- 2. Construct variables ---------------------------------------
ami[, treated  := (early_cath == 1 | early_pci == 1 | early_cabg == 1)]

# High-intensity hospital list constructed externally; merge flag
hi_hosp <- fread("hi_intensity_hospitals.csv")   # columns: provider_id, hi_intensity
ami <- merge(ami, hi_hosp, by = "provider_id", all.x = TRUE)
ami[is.na(hi_intensity), hi_intensity := 0]

# Instrument: differential distance
# Assume variables dist_hi, dist_lo already computed
ami[, diffdist := dist_hi - dist_lo]   # negative = closer to hi-intensity

# Basic covariates
covars <- c("age", "female", "race_black", "race_hisp",
            "dual_eligible", "diabetes", "hypertension",
            "prior_ami", "copd", "zip_median_income")

# Fixed effects identifiers
ami[, county_year := interaction(county_fips, admit_year)]

# --- 3. 2SLS main specification -----------------------------------
form_main <- as.formula(
  paste0("survival_5yr ~ 1 | 0 | (treated ~ diffdist) | ",
         paste(c(covars, "county_year"), collapse = "+"))
)

iv_main <- feols(form_main, data = ami, vcov = "cluster[provider_id]")
etable(iv_main, se.below = TRUE, title = "IV: Effect of Early Invasive Treatment on 5-Year Survival")

# --- 4. First stage check -----------------------------------------
fs <- feols(treated ~ diffdist + age + female + county_year, data = ami, vcov = "cluster[provider_id]")
summary(fs)$ivfstat

# --- 5. Robustness: rural subsample -------------------------------
iv_rural <- feols(form_main, data = ami[rural_zip == 1], vcov = "cluster[provider_id]")

# --- 6. Event-study robustness around hospital adoption -----------
# create relative_year_to_adoption variable prior to estimation
ami[, relyear := admit_year - hosp_adopt_year]
event <- feols(survival_5yr ~ i(relyear, ref = -1) + covars | provider_id + admit_year,
               data = ami[abs(relyear) <= 5])
iplot(event, ci = TRUE) + theme_minimal()

# --- 7. Balance test (falsification) ------------------------------
balance <- feols(cbind(age, diabetes, prior_ami) ~ diffdist | county_year,
                 data = ami, vcov = "cluster[county_year]")
etable(balance, title = "Balance across Instrument")
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Economic theory and prior clinical studies suggest that for *marginal* elderly patients the benefit of early invasive therapy is positive but modest.  
• Sign (+):  invasive procedures reopen occluded arteries, limiting infarct size, thus improving survival.  
• Magnitude:  I expect a Local Average Treatment Effect of ≈ +4–6 percentage points on 5-year survival (baseline ≈ 50–55 %).  Short-term gains (30-day survival) might be slightly smaller (~2 pp) because much mortality in the first days reflects massive infarctions that invasive therapy cannot fully avert.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV design)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1. Relevance (strong first-stage) ....................................... 1  
C2. Independence of instrument from potential outcomes (exogeneity) ...... 0.8  
C3. Exclusion of alternative channels (exclusion restriction) ............ 0.7  
C4. Monotonicity (no defiers) ........................................... 1  
C5. SUTVA / no spillovers ............................................... 1  

Overall → 4.5 / 5.  Remaining concerns center on exclusion (T3) and exogeneity (T1); addressed via controls, falsification tests, and robustness subsamples.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
This plan delivers a defensible causal estimate of how much early intensive cardiac care improves long-run survival among elderly AMI patients and decomposes which procedural components drive the gains.
